displayQuote: To love is to burn, to be on fire

meta.title: Who really said "To love is to burn, to be on fire"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Marianne Dashwood says it in the 1995 film, and the real line does not stop there. Emma Thompson wrote it, not Austen.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To love is to burn, to be on fire'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Austen — Emma Thompson, scene 51. And the sentence keeps going after “on fire”.

answer.label: Not Jane Austen — actually Emma Thompson
answer.authorDates: born 15 April 1959 · English actress and screenwriter
answer.sourceLine: Marianne Dashwood’s line in the 1995 Sense and Sensibility, written by Emma Thompson. The published screenplay ↗ has it at scene 51, and the full sentence runs on: “To love is to burn — to be on fire, all made of passion, of adoration, of sacrifice! Like Juliet, or Guinevere or Heloise —”. The popular version cuts it at the fifth word, which turns a girl’s overheated manifesto into a greetings-card maxim. Nothing resembling it is in Austen.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Marianne Dashwood (Kate Winslet) — a fictional character

source.excerpt:
MARIANNE: Can he love her? Can the ardour of the soul really be satisfied with such polite, concealed affections? To love is to burn — to be on fire, all made of passion, of adoration, of sacrifice! Like Juliet, or Guinevere or Heloise —
MRS DASHWOOD: They made rather pathetic ends, dear.
MARIANNE: Pathetic! To die for love? How can you say so? What could be more glorious?
trail: Searched all eight Austen texts at Project Gutenberg, including Sense and Sensibility ↗, for “to love is to burn” and “to be on fire”. Zero matches in either case.
Found the line in the full text of Emma Thompson, The Sense and Sensibility Screenplay & Diaries (Newmarket Press, 1995) ↗ at scene 51, in the longer form quoted above.

Cross-checked against Wikiquote’s transcription of the film ↗, which also gives the line to Marianne. Its wording differs slightly from the published script — Wikiquote transcribes what is heard on screen, the book prints the shooting script — so we quote the book and note the difference rather than treating either as the other.
Credits and release date confirmed against Wikipedia’s article on the film ↗.
source.excerptNote: Keep reading past the famous fragment. Mrs Dashwood’s flat reply is the point of the scene: the film is gently mocking Marianne’s theory of love, not endorsing it. Quoted alone, the line loses the joke it was written to set up.

source.rightsNote: In copyright. The published screenplay’s own copyright page states “Screenplay and all other text copyright © 1995 by Columbia Pictures Industries, Inc.”, with only the diaries copyright to Emma Thompson personally — the standard work-for-hire split for screen writing. Austen’s 1811 novel is public domain, but this line is not from it.

author.bio: Emma Thompson (born 15 April 1959) is an English actress and screenwriter. Her adaptation of Sense and Sensibility won the Academy Award for Best Adapted Screenplay at the 68th Academy Awards, making her the only person to have won Oscars for both acting and screenwriting. She also plays Elinor Dashwood in the film.

copyAttribution: Jane Austen did not write “To love is to burn, to be on fire.” Emma Thompson wrote it for Marianne Dashwood in the 1995 film of Sense and Sensibility (published screenplay, scene 51), and the real line continues: “…all made of passion, of adoration, of sacrifice! Like Juliet, or Guinevere or Heloise —”. Via quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Two things are wrong with this quotation as it circulates: the author, and the full stop.

items.why: Neither “to love is to burn” nor “to be on fire” occurs anywhere in Austen’s fiction ↗.
Scene 51 of her published 1995 screenplay ↗, spoken by Marianne Dashwood.
The script reads “To love is to burn — to be on fire, all made of passion, of adoration, of sacrifice! Like Juliet, or Guinevere or Heloise —”. The dash becomes a comma and the rest disappears.

misattribution.truthLine: The line is Emma Thompson’s, it belongs to a seventeen-year-old being teased for melodrama, and in the script ↗ it does not end where the internet ends it.

context.heading: A manifesto, not a maxim
lead: Marianne is the novel’s argument against exactly this view of love. Thompson’s scene compresses that argument into a few lines: Marianne declares that love must burn, invokes Juliet and Guinevere and Heloise, and her mother replies that they all came to sticky ends.
Sheared of its second half and its punchline, the sentence gets shared as advice. In its source it is a symptom — the thing Marianne has to survive before the story will let her be happy.
context.pull: They made rather pathetic ends, dear.
